note: std::set dedups on insert at O(log n) each; sort-then-unique dedups a vector in one O(n log n) pass.
The recursive version recomputes every subproblem exponentially; the loop computes each one exactly once.
Swapping to i-k-j strides sequentially through both b's row and c's row, which is far more cache-friendly.
The textbook i-j-k loop order strides down each column of B, which is the cache-unfriendly access pattern.
Hand-split threads need a manual join and combine step that std::reduce(par) does for you internally.
call_once with a static once_flag guarantees the initialiser runs exactly once, even racing across threads.
A function-local static is guaranteed thread-safe initialisation since C++11; the raw pointer version is not.
std::accumulate is the STL name for reduce; both compile down to the same loop with -O2.
std::reduce with an execution policy may sum out of order, which is only safe when addition truly commutes here.
std::swap uses move assignment under the hood, so it is never slower than the hand-written version.
